title: CRDTs
description: Understand Conflict-free Replicated Data Types without the math: G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set, LWW-Register, and when CRDTs solve real problems versus when they don't.

segments.text: What if I told you there's a data structure that never needs conflict resolution? No last-write-wins, no merge functions, no coordination. Multiple replicas update independently, and when they sync, they automatically converge to the same state. These are CRDTs, and they're not magic. They're math you can use without understanding the proofs.

Start with the simplest one: the G-Counter, a grow-only counter. Each replica maintains its own count. Replica A increments its slot, Replica B increments its slot. To read the total, sum all slots. To merge, take the max of each slot. It can only go up, but that's perfect for page view counters, like counts, or ad impression tracking.

Need to decrement too? The PN-Counter uses two G-Counters internally: one for increments, one for decrements. The value is the positive counter minus the negative counter. Both merge independently using the G-Counter max rule. Now you have a counter that goes up and down without any coordination. Shopping cart quantities, upvote-downvote scores, inventory counts.

The LWW-Register is the controversial one. Last Writer Wins. Each update carries a timestamp, and the highest timestamp wins during merge. Simple, but dangerous. If two users update a profile name at the same wall clock time, one update silently disappears. Clock skew between servers makes this even worse. Use it only when losing an update is acceptable.
segments.thought_prompt: Can you think of a scenario where silently dropping a write would cause real business damage?

segments.text: The OR-Set, observed-remove set, solves the add-remove conflict. Each add generates a unique tag. Remove only removes tags the replica has seen. If Replica A adds 'milk' and Replica B removes 'milk' concurrently, add wins because B's remove only targets tags B has observed. This matches user intuition: if I added something, it should be there.

Riak was the poster child for CRDTs in production. They shipped counters, sets, maps, and flags as first-class data types. Write to any node, reads converge automatically. Their customers used CRDT counters for real-time analytics and CRDT sets for user permissions across globally distributed clusters.

Redis Enterprise also uses CRDTs for their active-active geo-replication. When you increment a counter in the Tokyo cluster and decrement it in Virginia simultaneously, they converge without conflict. Redis chose CRDTs specifically because they eliminate the need for cross-region coordination, which would add hundreds of milliseconds of latency.

Now the hard truth. CRDTs can't do everything. They can't enforce global invariants like 'inventory must not go negative.' They can't do transactions across multiple CRDTs atomically. And they accumulate metadata: an OR-Set must remember every tombstoned tag forever, or until garbage collection, which requires coordination. The very thing you wanted to avoid.
segments.thought_prompt: If CRDTs can't enforce 'inventory >= 0', how would you handle overselling in a distributed e-commerce system?

segments.text: Use CRDTs when you need availability over consistency, when operations are commutative, and when you can tolerate eventual convergence. Collaborative editing, distributed counters, shopping carts, presence indicators. Don't use them for bank balances, seat reservations, or anything needing strong consistency.

CRDTs are one of those tools that seem niche until you need them, and then they're exactly right. They turn the coordination problem on its head: instead of agreeing before writing, you write freely and agree on how to merge. That shift in thinking is the real lesson here.
